#3352. Patrick Stewart’s Most Infamous Flop Officially Returns to Netflix

Erielle Sudario is a Collider News and Feature Author from Australia and has worked in the journalism industry since 2018. She has a passion for entertainment and pop culture news and has interviewed YouTubers, voice actors, film directors, and musicians throughout her career. When she's not writing, you can see Erielle building keyboards, reading a good book, playing video games, and creating content on social media.

Sir Patrick Stewart was a renowned actor who starred in many projects. While he may be known for his science fiction and superhero work in franchises like Star Trek and X-Men, he has also done several surprising projects that showcase his talent as an actor, like voicing Avery Bullock in American Dad!. After the legendary actor passed earlier this year, Avengers: Doomsday is set to be his final role, but one of his most unlikely — and worst-rated — films is officially resurfacing ahead of the holidays.

It's no secret that Hollywood is a business, with studios investing in projects they believe will succeed. However, as the recent shakeup at DC Studios suggests, their definition of success doesn't always align with audiences' expectations. Beyond revisiting established franchises through sequels, spin-offs, and reboots, Hollywood also looks to capitalize on popular trends. One example is the upcoming Labubu movie, based on Pop Mart's sought-after collectible plush, despite their recent decline in popularity. But before this movie was greenlit, another trend-driven film was released in theaters nearly 10 years ago, and even Sir Patrick Stewart had a role in the feature.

In 2017, Sony Pictures released The Emoji Movie, which follows a "meh" Emoji named Gene (T.J. Miller), who's on the run after he can't pull the "meh" face during a text. Hoping to become normal, he sets out to find a "hacker" to fix him so he can be a normal emoji. The Emoji Movie features a star-studded cast, including James Corden as Hi-5, the high-five emoji, Maya Rudolph as Smiler, a Smiley Emoji, Jennifer Coolidge as Mary Meh, Gene's mother, and Stewart voicing the Poop Emoji. The Emoji Movie was heavily criticized, but it generated over $217.8 million at the global box office, surpassing its $50 million budget. Next month, The Emoji Movie will be returning to Netflix, just in time for Stewart fans to binge the actor's entire filmography, including the bad ones, before Avengers: Doomsday comes out.

Since its release, The Emoji Movie has received overwhelmingly negative reviews, earning a 6% critics' score and a 36% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, alongside a 1.5-star rating on Letterboxd. Critics described The Emoji Movie as "pointless," criticized its excessive product placement, and argued that it struggled to "express" itself despite featuring a wide range of emojis. While many advised audiences to avoid the movie, a handful of critics praised it, with one calling it "one of the boldest mainstream American movies in ages" and another describing it as "inventive." Despite its box office success, The Emoji Movie was widely regarded as one of the worst films of 2017.

The Emoji Movie enters Netflix on December 1, 2026. Follow Collider for more updates.

#3351. AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” an upcoming film from YouTuber Gossip Goblin that was made entirely with generated artificial intelligence, was deemed ineligible for the Best Animated Feature Oscar at the upcoming Academy Awards.

As IndieWire previously reported on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” which is the first fully AI movie to be released theatrically, the film had submitted for consideration and had planned FYC screenings alongside its theatrical release on December 4.

But the film was not included among the list of 38 animated films deemed eligible for this year’s Oscars that were announced Monday, November 23. IndieWire understands that the Academy’s Animation Branch Executive Committee determined “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” did not meet the Academy’s definition of an animated film under the rules for the 99th Awards. Related Stories The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

Here’s the full rule as written that the Academy felt “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” did not satisfy:

An animated film is one in which characters or objects are given the illusion of life by having movement created for them, by any human means. While the crucial movement of a live-action motion picture is captured at speed, animation is the craft of human creation and manipulation of images to produce a performance from inanimate objects. At least 75 percent of the motion picture’s running time, without opening or end credits, must include animation of the primary subject or subjects. An animated feature has a running time of more than 40 minutes. Upon submission, filmmakers must provide information supporting how the motion picture qualifies as an animated film.

Edward Saatchi, a producer on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” with Fable Studios, told IndieWire he and director Zack London (a.k.a. Gossip Goblin) plan to appeal the animation branch’s decision and cited the example of Richard Linklater’s rotoscoped film “Apollo 10 1/2,” which was originally deemed ineligible but saw the branch reverse its decision upon appeal. Saatchi said that the film, in addition to submitting for Best Animated Feature, also submitted in other categories such as Best Director, Adapted Screenplay, VFX, and Sound. But if the film doesn’t fall under the animation branch today, he believes eventually AI movies will inevitably find a place somewhere within Academy rules, even if it ends up being a theoretical “Best AI Movie” category.

“‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ is starting a big debate around where cinematic works of art made with AI fit. Is it time to consider a ‘Best AI Movie?’ Do these films fit best in the voice-actor led animation category? Is AI simply the new VFX? It’s going to take the whole industry time to figure it out,” Saatchi said. “With traditional garlanded directors like Matthieu Kassovitz, Alex Proyas, and Doug Liman making heavily-AI films, it’s going to be a good debate of how to categorize. We think Best Animated is simplest, but it may be the Academy decides ultimately that a Best AI movie category will make the most sense with these films where everything you’re seeing is generative.”

Of note, one of the films that did qualify for Best Animated Feature was “Coyote vs. Acme,” which is a hybrid animated and live-action film featuring the Looney Tunes alongside human actors in the real world. The Academy on Monday also announced the eligible features in the Best Documentary Feature race and the Best International Feature race.

As part of the Academy’s most recent rules changes from earlier this year, only roles credited in the film’s legal billing that are demonstrably performed by humans with their consent are eligible for acting categories, and screenplays must be human-authored to be eligible. That rule changed followed on guidelines from last year ahead of the 98th Oscars in which the Academy specified, “[Gen-AI] tools neither help nor harm the chances of achieving a nomination. The Academy and each branch will judge the achievement, taking into account the degree to which a human was at the heart of the creative authorship when choosing which movie to award.”

In the case of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” the film has a script written by London, and though all the characters in the film are generated with AI visually, it features real human actors doing the voice work for the characters. The film also features cameos of some real-life people playing parts resembling themselves, most notably the pop star Grimes. But the film has elaborate look books, visual reference points, and photo mashing that all went into the creation of these characters, something that clearly has human authorship and goes beyond a computer interpreting a single prompt.

Part of Gossip Goblin’s battle in legitimizing “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is in showing there was a human team, between 30-35 people, working for years on the film’s creation. Gossip Goblin also recently released a behind-the-scenes documentary that showcases the film’s composer, its foley artist, its voice actors, and more detailing the human effort that went into the project.

Discussion over AI in Oscar eligible films came to a head after several movies in the 2024 Oscar race were reported to have included AI in their post-production editing process, including “A Complete Unknown,” “The Brutalist,” and “Emilia Pérez.” The examples were for traditional VFX, not for anything that enhanced or altered performances, but the Academy as a result now requires disclosure of AI if it is used in a film.

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts” begins its theatrical run on December 4, which will initially be an Oscar-qualifying run, and it will expand on January 22 alongside a rollout with the film’s international distributor AGC International.

#3350. Eight Important Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand new or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

Your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

Some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

While some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

The password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

Being able to log into your router's admin dashboard from anywhere may be useful if you have complex networking needs or troubleshooting issues that often have to be addressed when you're away from home, but it also leaves an entry point open for attackers. Turn off remote management to prevent anyone from accessing your dashboard unless they are on your network. (This is also a great reason to have strong, unique admin credentials.)

Two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets users connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.

#3348. The iPhone Duo Is Getting Face Unlock

Apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is currently beta testing the third major update in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other new features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first new iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This update just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software update can introduce new hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

What's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

Apple made a big deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That said, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some users may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the new option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

#3347. Why Is the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Trailer So… Gloomy? Internet Erupts Over Latest Look at Marvel Movie

There’s a storm brewing, chere, and it has nothing to do with the weird Gambit (Channing Tatum) and Herbie the Robot Dunkin Donuts ads that played like once a quarter during all the football games on Sunday.

The final trailer was released ahead of Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday,” the mega-Sentinel, crossover-tastic 165-minute Russo Brothers opus out on December 18. And the response hasn’t been great — in part because Cyclops says, “To me, my X-Men!” and there isn’t actually a Storm.

Way back in the salad days of 2012, Joss Whedon first did an “Assemble” shot that roved in a circle all of the original “Avengers” film, while an Alan Silvestri score bwaaamped the brassy “Avengers” theme. Say whatever you like about Whedon’s strengths and weaknesses when it comes to visual style, but the first time this happened, the shot’s continuous nature served a storytelling purpose. It was the cinematic way to finally bind these crazy kids together in superhero fellowship — through the timeless crucible of New York City getting shredded into CGI bits by alien-monster things. Related Stories AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch

But over the many, many Phases of the MCU, the Avengers Assemble shots have kept happening. And happening. And sure enough, the “Doomsday” trailer crescendos with a bunch of our heroes stuck in a gray-black wasteland void that looks like a glitched “Expedition 33” loading screen, with the camera straining to create that same sense of unity.

It doesn’t. At least not in the trailer. Which is why so much of the response to the finale “Doomsday” trailer has been focused on it.

As folks online have pointed out, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) looks like he’s standing in entirely different lighting from the people closest to him. There’s no sense of texture or proximity that suggests anybody was placed against the same green screen together, let alone acting together (a problem that has been pointed out about the filmmaking process for “Doomsday” already).

No amount of money can make up for shooting for maximum flexibility — which so often can devolve into being indecisive — or for pursuing relentless revisions throughout the VFX pipeline. That is exactly what leads to shadowy, sloppily-framed environments like wherever the hell the Avengers are fighting Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) and his creations. And because the environment is so flattened and indistinct, only the barest hints of color survive. And really, only because Reed Richards (Pedro Pascal) is still wearing a coat from a different movie.

Now, what comes most naturally to Cyclops is shooting an optic blast from his eyes, and what comes most naturally to us is posting negative takes online. The trailer takes that shot out of context for nostalgia’s sake; its dramatic purpose within the film itself might be more complicated, or the setup for a twist in three different timelines’ worth of Avengers’ fortunes. But when it comes to all the cinematic crimes of artless visuals, repetitive plots, and overbearing lore that have contributed to superhero fatigue? The “Avengers: Doomsday” trailer doesn’t seem to be beating the charges.

#3344. Netflix's 6-Part Dystopian Series Is A Masterclass In Updating Classic Sci-Fi

While one of Netflix’s best dystopian sci-fi shows had a long and tricky road to the small screen, the investment was worth it in the end thanks to the show’s triumphant debut season. Sci-fi TV is currently enjoying a golden era in the 2020s. While the ‘90s had classics like The X-Files and Star Trek: The Next Generation, the advent of streaming services has opened up a whole new world of small-screen sci-fi storytelling.

On Apple TV alone, there is Invasion, Monarch: Legacy of Monsters, Foundation, Dark Matter, Severance, Murderbot, and the Colin Farrell vehicle Sugar, a high profile hit that doesn’t even reveal its sci-fi elements until an audacious plot twist midway through season 1. On Netflix, Stranger Things, Black Mirror, and 3 Body Problem have all expanded the possibilities of small-screen sci-fi’s scope and scale, while Hulu’s Margaret Atwood adaptation The Handmaid’s Tale managed to expand on the iconic novel's story without losing the show’s critical acclaim.

Not one to be outdone, Netflix offered viewers a dystopian adaptation of its own in early 2025, and this six-season season had a historically long and rocky road to the screen. Based on the classic 1957 comic book of the same name, The Eternaut is an Argentinian sci-fi show that follows a group of survivors navigating a sudden, catastrophic alien invasion of their home city of Buenos Aires.

Penned by Héctor Germán Oesterheld (HGO) and Francisco Solano López, the comic series El Eternauta was first published between 1957 and 1959. The comic follows a group of survivors in the aftermath of a deadly alien invasion, and the comic was remade in 1969 with a revision that made its political messaging more explicit. After HGO was disappeared by Argentina’s fascist government, the rights to his most influential work went to his widow.

There was a failed attempt to mount an animated adaptation of El Eternauta during HGO’s life, but only an expensive pilot of this proposed adaptation was ever produced. Despite plentiful interest in a potential movie adaptation, complex copyright issues and the author’s uncertainty about translating the story’s political allegories to an English-speaking, non-Argentinian context stalled any potential developments.

In the years that followed, the dystopian masterpiece The Eternaut was repeatedly almost adapted, only for various practicalities to stall its production. In 1995, a live-action miniseries was almost funded before it was abandoned, while, in 2007, The Headless Woman director Lucrecia Martel was hired to write a screenplay, only for producers to leave the project in limbo after over a year of development.

Finally, As Luck Would Have It director Álex de la Iglesia began working on an adaptation of The Eternaut in 2018 and, although this wasn’t the version viewers received from Netflix, its development kick-started the show that was finally released in 2025. Created by Pizza, biro, faso director Bruno Stagnaro, Netflix’s The Eternaut maintained de la Iglesia’s choice of leading man, Ricardo Darín, in role of Juan Salvo.

Perhaps emboldened by the critical success of HBO’s dystopian shows Station Eleven and The Last of Us, Netflix released The Eternaut to widespread critical acclaim in 2025. Although season 1 did depart from its source material with the addition of Ariel Staltari’s new character Omar, The Eternaut was still widely celebrated as a faithful and intelligent, but also enthralling and exciting adaptation of the seminal comic.

Now that HGO’s iconic comic has finally found its way to the screen, viewers of season 1 will be delighted to hear that the show will only go from strength to strength in its sophomore outing. Netflix renewed The Eternaut for a second season in May 2025, and the source material offers more answers to its many mysteries as its story continues.

Erielle Sudario is a Collider News and Feature Author from Australia and has worked in the journalism industry since 2018. Does every villain need a backstory reveal? No. But with Hollywood revisiting existing stories and old IP, it seems even the bad guys need a second chance. Recently, Netflix released a film based on a popular fairy tale, but from a different character's perspective, and it has become a streaming hit. The fairy tale in question is Cinderella, a story about a young girl forced into servitude by her evil stepmother and stepsisters; with the help of her Fairy Godmother, she goes to the ball and dances with the prince, but must leave before midnight. After leaving her glass slipper behind, the prince searches the kingdom for his true love and eventually reunites with Cinderella.

​​​​​​​This fairy tale has been adapted many times, including Disney, so much so that the character made her way to the Descendants franchise, revealing that Cinderella and the Prince have children. Recently, Netflix released an animated children's fantasy film called Steps, a retelling of Cinderella from the perspective of one of Cinderella's stepsisters, Lilith, voiced by Ali Wong. Steps was released on Netflix on November 20, 2026, and has since become a streaming hit, reaching #2 on Netflix's Top 10 Movie Charts Worldwide, between Guarding Stars and Heartland. Alongside its streaming success, Steps was well-received by fans and critics alike, earning a 78% critics score and a 71% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.

Steps follows Lilith, one of Cinderella's stepsisters, whose family is treated as outsiders while Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) earns the kingdom's sympathy following her father's death. The movie puts a twist on the classic fairy tale when Lilith steals the Fairy Godmother's (Bette Midler) wand and crashes the royal ball with her sister, Margot. However, things take another turn when Cinderella's rival, Priscilla (Nikki Glaser), steals the wand and uses its magic to make the prince fall in love with her and seize control of the kingdom. Now, Lilith and Cinderella must put aside their differences and work together to restore order.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Steps isn't the only Cinderella retelling that puts the stepsisters in the spotlight. Back in 2007, Disney released Cinderella III: A Twist in Time. Like Steps, the movie features Cinderella's stepsister, Anastasia (Tress MacNeille), stealing the Fairy Godmother's (Russi Taylor) wand, and Lady Tremaine (Susanne Blakeslee), Cinderella's evil stepmother, using its magic to travel back in time and change the original movie's events, ensuring Anastasia marries the prince instead and leaving Cinderella (Jennifer Hale) to set things right.

While both movies feature a stepsister stealing a magic wand, Steps follows Lilith and Cinderella as they reconcile their differences and rebuild their relationship. Meanwhile, the Disney version has Anastasia learning that she wants to find her own true love rather than force someone to love her through magic. She eventually reconciles with Cinderella, while Drizella and Lady Tremaine face punishment for their actions.

Steps is available to stream on Netflix. Follow Collider for more updates.

If you're having trouble accessing your bank right now, you aren't alone. As of Monday afternoon, a number of banks are experiencing outages and interruptions to service.

#3341. Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:

In fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

#3339. 10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?)

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

If you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

#3338. Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign sounds like exactly what I’ve been wanting

Rumors about next year’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models have been ramping up, and they suggest Apple is designing an ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ that combines traits from two current models.

Apple keeps expanding the iPhone line to include new models. And while it’s great that there are more models for differing preferences and needs, it’s also left me missing the days of having one model that was the clear “best.”

That problem isn’t going away, since the iPhone Duo represents a brand new type of iPhone that some users will love, while others find it isn’t for them.

With my failed iPhone Duo experiment over, I’m back to using iPhone 18 Pro as my default model. But I still have an iPhone Air around for work, and every time I pick it up, I’m struck by how impressive it remains.

I used the iPhone Air all of last year and loved it. The main reason I upgraded to an iPhone 18 Pro is the camera system. I have young children at home—including newborn twins—and want to capture the best possible photos before they get older.

iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera has been fantastic, and it’s great having the Telephoto again too.

But I still sorely miss the overall design of the iPhone Air. And it sounds like next year, I could get the best of both models.

Rumors indicate Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models will have a unique new design featuring a quad-curved display that makes it look bezel-free.

The new models are expected to also be a bit slimmer, use curved edges, and possibly even bring back titanium. Leakers say the new design borrows a lot from the iPhone Air’s look.

This sounds like exactly what I’ve been hoping for.

If they make one the size of the iPhone 13 mini I will buy. Otherwise I'm holding out

While the ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ certainly won’t—and shouldn’t—be as thin as iPhone Air, if it can slim down a little and adopt several other Air design traits, I suspect it will evoke the same affection the Air has.

But unlike the Air, the new Pro model will still offer the best camera system in an iPhone (not to mention better battery life).

As a huge fan of the design of the Air, and the functionality of the 18 Pro, Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone model could prove the perfect model for me. And for anyone else not opting for iPhone Duo 2.

What do you think of the rumored iPhone 20 Pro design? Let us know in the comments.

#3336. Star Trek: Divergent Timeline Officially Brings Back The Kelvin Era Crew

Star Trek can boldly go wherever it pleases, but right now there doesn't seem to be a heading. Following the conclusion of multiple Star Trek series in recent history, there isn't a clear mainline direction, and all the spinoffs seem short-lived as Paramount retools its entire media division.

That said, there are plenty of Star Trek stories to enjoy throughout the decades. The series has been around for so long that countless creatives have taken cracks at it, some of whom are better at navigating deep space than others. But if you're a fan of the Kelvin Timeline, you're in luck, as Star Trek: Divergent Timeline is bringing them back with a recent release.

In case you haven't been following Star Trek, the Kelvin Timeline was introduced in 2009's film simply titled Star Trek, directed by J.J. Abrams and starring Chris Pine as James T. Kirk.

In essence, in the year 2387, the Romulan Nero travels back to 2233 and destroys the USS Kelvin, along with First Officer George Kirk. This splits the timeline, creating the alternate universe many refer to as the "Kelvin Timeline." It's garnered a mixed reception since its original release (especially in terms of its sequel, Into Darkness), but it still has fans, and it's part of Star Trek's decades-long history.

That timeline is now making it into Magic: The Gathering, as shared by Wizards of the Coast officially:

Experience 60 years of Klingons, Vulcans, Tamarians, and more with Magic: The Gathering® | Star Trek™! Magic's latest set puts the stories and characters that have captivated generations front and center, celebrating the legacy and future of the Star Trek franchise with Booster Fun treatments like borderless scene cards. Each scene card is part of a larger, multi-card piece that depicts a corner of the Star Trek universe, whether that's an iconic episode or an especially chaotic moment on the bridge. Here are all the scenes you can find in this set!

Multiple crew members have made it onto the set, topped off by a release called Divergent Timeline, which reunites the film trilogy crew in scene cards. So here's what we're getting with Divergent Timeline:

JB Casacop's scene aboard the Enterprise features Kirk, Spock, Uhura, and more, but they look a tad different here! This is the Kelvin timeline, depicted in 2009's Star Trek and other films. You'll also find these incarnations of the crew on the set's Stardates cards.

In other words, we're getting Captain Kirk, as well as Spock, Uhura, Chekov and McCoy, Scotty, and Sulu, as they appear in their Kelvin Timeline forms in the feature films. They bear the likenesses of the films, in line with the rest of the sets.

The other big scene card addition includes Enterprise-Q, depicting the chaos of this particular episode when Q meddled with the Enterprise. Depicted by ALexandaar Gering, it gives us a close look at the Next Generation crew, including the iconic Jean-Luc Picard. Even if Star Trek is rudderless in the years to come, it's had plenty of celebrations so far that are worth remembering.

#3335. The 13 Best Christmas Movies of the Last 5 Years, Ranked

Christmas and the holiday season have proven to be a time-honored tradition and a great setting for several beloved and cheerful films that perfectly use the festivities to create timeless classics. It's become a staple of many households to put on some of the most iconic and beloved holiday films for the season, with a great number of highly memorable Christmas films to choose from. However, while it always works to put on a classic like Home Alone, National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation, and Elf, there are still a great number of holiday films being created during the modern era.

While it may seem like a Herculean task to create a modern Christmas film that can live up to the undeniable stature of the many classics, a few successfully create similar cozy feelings perfect for the season. While no Christmas film can attain the legacy and strengths of its predecessors, the best and most iconic Christmas films of the modern era act as a great addition to the zeitgeist of the holiday season on film.

Animated family Christmas films have been a long-lasting trend in holiday filmmaking for decades, with a wide array of different filmmakers utilizing the medium to bring to life feel-good stories of holiday cheer and whimsy. While That Christmas doesn't break the mold or stray too far from the traditional values of animated Christmas films past, its inherent earnestness, combined with an array of lovable vocal performances, makes it one of the most underrated animated holiday films of recent memory.

The film follows an array of different storylines that intertwine with one another, almost acting like an animated equivalent to Love Actually, another film written by acclaimed screenwriter Richard Curtis. Animation proves to work with this style of storytelling tremendously, especially when the connecting link that brings all of these stories together is a disastrous snowstorm that vastly alters everyone's individual holiday plans. While it may not be as iconic as Curtis's other holiday films, it certainly has the potential to be a hidden holiday gem of the modern era.

A goofy, musical comedy adaptation of the holiday classic A Christmas Carol, Spirited provides just the right amount of comic absurdism and charm to make for a compelling, modern rendition of the Dickens classic. The inherent chemistry and dynamic between Ryan Reynolds as a Scrooge-styled media consultant and Will Ferrell as the Ghost of Christmas Present is enough to make for a joyously fun comedic time. The musical aspects of the film also work surprisingly well, with the entire supporting cast able to bring the holiday spirit required to make its musical numbers so cheery and infectious.

While the film has been largely overlooked and overshadowed due to being an Apple TV original, it has slowly amassed a reputation as one of the more entertaining and approachable Christmas Carol adaptations of the modern era. Its inherent concept of the Scrooge-archetype character flipping the script of A Christmas Carol back onto the ghosts immediately distinguishes the film from other adaptations, giving it a niche that will help it considerably as time goes on.

One of many prominent comedies from director Michael Showalter, Oh. What. Fun. sets itself up as a Christmas movie playing to the appeals and struggles of mothers, specifically mothers who are not thanked or appreciated for the work they put into the family. Michelle Pfeiffer in the leading role plays this perfectly, as she plays a family matriarch who is fed up with her family after being left home alone, deciding to set off on her own adventure and leaving her family scrambling to find her.

While Pfeiffer herself is the major draw and strength of the film, it's the comedic chemistry and dynamic of the entire supporting cast that makes Oh. What. Fun. such an engaging modern Christmas film. The likes of Denis Leary, Felicity Jones, Dominic Sessa, Jason Schwarzman, and Chloë Grace Moretz each add their own signature charms and strengths to make this one of the most memorable Christmas movies of the streaming era.

One of several successful parody slashers from writer Michael Kennedy, best known for his work writing Freaky and Heart Eyes, It's a Wonderful Knife brings the energy and scares of a horror slasher to the base premise of the all-time Christmas classic It's a Wonderful Life. The film sees a young teen (Jane Widdop) still reeling from the pain and trauma of having saved her town from a psychotic killer on Christmas Eve. However, when she wishes that she were never born, she ends up transported to a parallel world where the killings never stopped and have gone on non-stop for a full year.

While a lot of the film hinges on the ingenuity and intrigue of its wild parody premise, there are a lot of inherent strengths that help give the film its own identity beyond simply being a cheesy parody. Most notably is the hilariously over-the-top villain performance from Justin Long, who, complete with a goofy high-pitched Southern accent, steals the show. The film also doesn't shy away from brazen and openly LGBTQ+ themes and characters, being much more accepting than the average slasher or Christmas film.

Even just describing the plot of the film simply doesn't do justice to Hot Frosty's chaotic and absurdist nature, as it's the type of wild, nonsensical experience that simply needs to be seen to be believed. The film follows a young widow living painfully alone during the holiday season before unexpectedly bringing an attractive, male model snowman to life with a magic scarf. She finds herself doing her best not just to make sure the snowman doesn't get into trouble, but also keeping her feelings in check as he slowly but surely begins to warm her heart.

Taking the mythos and fantasy concepts of the holiday season and creating a massive blockbuster experience with a $250 million budget out of it, Red One is arguably the first film that comes to mind for general audiences when considering memorable holiday films of the past few years. This Dwayne Johnson and Chris Evans-led blockbuster made waves by initially releasing in theaters in early November before having a massive streaming release right in time for the holiday season.

It certainly does a good job of replicating the feel and energy of a modern blockbuster, seamlessly implementing classic Christmas elements and transforming them for modern, digital-technology times. The action comedy strives for mass appeal above all else, playing to the strengths of its leading stars and certainly having fun in its execution as they deal with the goofiness of Christmas magic on a massive blockbuster scale.

Not for the faint of heart, even for die-hard horror fans, Terrifier 3 brings the same level of shockingly gruesome gore and violence that the previous films provided, yet with the added texture and energy of the holiday season. The film fully commits to the iconography and energy of the holiday season, whether it be through Art dressing up as Santa for a large chunk of his kills or using holiday-themed weaponry to create maximum carnage. It builds upon the chaos and energy of previous entries to make for a gruesomely good time, although it's definitely the type of Christmas film not meant to be watched by the whole family.

Terrifier 3 is easily at its best when it allows Art to play into the madness and absurdity of holiday slashers as a whole, even when many of his antics are absolutely sickening and abhorrent to watch unfold. While many simply won't be able to handle the overwhelming gore and sadistic pain that the film presents, it's a shockingly good time for those who are accustomed to this style of gruesome slasher. As far as modern holiday horror films are concerned, Terrifier 3 easily stands above the rest as the most entertaining and sickening of them all.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

A short yet sweet side story in the MCU, The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special sees Drax and Mantis setting out on a mission to make this Christmas unforgettable for Quill. The team heads off to Earth in search of the perfect present, but Earth proves to be a challenge to the hapless duo, leading to a great deal of chaotic Christmas mischief.

Despite its short runtime of less than an hour, The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special makes use of every available moment, filled with all the classic comedic greatness that the trilogy is so beloved for. It's a testament to the chemistry and dynamic between the Guardians as a whole and just how well they can adapt comedically to any situation, as they make a surprisingly perfect fit for holiday festivities. Its short runtime also makes it incredibly rewatchable, an easy and cozy film to have to put on and let loose for a while.

Violent Night sees a team of mercenaries break into a wealthy family's compound on Christmas Eve and take everyone inside hostage. However, the unthinkable happens, as Santa Claus finds himself on the premises in the middle of delivering presents. After the young child of the family calls out for Santa's help, he makes it his duty to go from nice to naughty and show the mercenaries a taste of their own medicine.

Action movies and Christmas go surprisingly hand in hand more often than not, especially for those who consider Die Hard a Christmas film. Violent Night fully commits to the comedic premise of "John Wick but with Santa Claus," with the perfect balance of silly hijinks and exhilarating action to make the film a cheerful blast to watch. Especially for those who are tired of the safer and wholesome energy that overwhelms the season, Violent Night provides enough high-octane brutality and action to bring joy to any Grinch's heart.

There really isn't an experience quite like a holiday get-together with extended family, as this charming gathering of beloved family members over sweets, games, and presents is all sorts of comforting, but has a hint of isolation in the most unlikely of places. It's this unique feeling and energy that Christmas Eve in Miller's Point seamlessly recaptures in its execution, showing both the beauty and the difficulties of the holiday with family in its own melancholy way.

The indie dramedy film certainly isn't as approachable as a traditional Christmas comedy, as it doesn't strive to have a major overarching plot, instead showing a scatterplot of moments and characters interacting with one another during the holiday season. However, in a way, this adds to the beauty of the film, because family get-togethers are never about linear stories, but are instead embraced and remembered for the feelings that they conjure up in us, and in that way, this film succeeds with flying colors.

#3331. The Best Early Black Friday Deals on DeWalt, Milwaukee, and Ryobi Cordless Power Tools

Becca Lewis is home maintenance writer who aims to foster confidence in and inspire DIY enthusiasts at all skill levels.

Becca attended Southern Connecticut State University, where she studied technical theater and design. She has a background in carpentry and fabrication and has worked in specialty shops, using a wide variety of tools and materials, for more than 20 years.

Becca has also written for Angi, where she specializes in creating guides for DIY, home maintenance, and renovations, and she indulges her love of sci-fi and fantasy by writing about entertainment and science for Giant Freakin Robot. She serves on the board of the Good Junk Sanctuary in Portland, Oregon, focusing on community engagement in the DIY and reuse space.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted home tool brand.

The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt cordless 20-volt cutout saw is on sale on Amazon for $102.95, 53% off its typical price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a 20-volt DeWalt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for custom trimming drywall, cutting custom shapes for going around outlet covers, or custom cutting trim in tight spaces.

The DeWalt 20-volt cordless angle grinder is on sale at Lowe’s for $209, 47% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a 4-amp-hour battery, but you’ll need a DeWalt 20-volt charger to use it. This is a good tool for metalworking or for grinding down screw tips that poke through or trimming bolt ends off.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. This is one of the most versatile cordless tools, allowing you to cut a wide range of materials and use a sanding attachment to do finishing work as well.

The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. #3326. Apple TV’s Masterpiece Spy Thriller Series With 4 Seasons On The Way Delivers A Masterclass In Tension

Apple TV is the home of many high-profile shows, including a spy thriller series that defies streaming rules in multiple ways, such as by having four confirmed seasons on the way, and it is a show that delivers a masterclass in tension for a few reasons. Apple TV has become the go-to for those searching for good production values and consistency in the age of streaming.

Apple TV tends to give shows the necessary time to develop, find their footing, and conclude their stories. In addition to that, it is the perfect streaming service for viewers who are looking for engaging, high-stakes, intense series. Multi-season projects that fit that bill include Severance, Silo, For All Mankind, and more, with not all of them being part of Apple TV's excellent sci-fi catalog.

Slow Horses, a spy thriller series, is certainly part of that group, and Apple TV recently confirmed how it might trust the gritty series more than any other project on its library of shows. After all, while Slow Horses season 6 recently concluded, the show is confirmed to return for at least four more seasons, up to season 10, and its delivery of a masterclass in tension is key to that.

Slow Horses has released six seasons so far on Apple TV, all of them consisting of just six episodes. This plays into how the show is so intense, as the spy thriller series is all plot, no filler, yet it packs quite a bit of much-needed character development without impacting the show's pacing. Another factor that ups the tension in this espionage story is the fact that nobody is safe, as both major characters and long-running supporting players have died over the course of Slow Horses' six seasons. Fans are left worrying about the fates of their favorites the whole time.

Another added layer of tension for the series comes from the fact that the agents of Slough House, while capable, are not near-perfect spies like James Bond. These are fallible characters who are known to make mistakes and misjudge situations, having to find ways to overcome the many challenges that arise along the way as they stumble upon major conspiracies. This both makes the show an exciting watch, but also a nerve-wracking espionage thriller. Finally, there is also the fact that Gary Oldman, one of the best actors alive, lights up the screen when Jackson Lamb drops the slacker act and means business.

Slow Horses has another four seasons on the way, but fans of the spy thriller series only have a good clue of what might happen in seasons 7 and 8. After all, the show is based on Mick Herron's series of novels, and there are currently only two more books left to be adapted, Bad Actors and Clown Town. A clear plot point set to be picked up and elevate the tension next season is the reveal of what will happen to Jack Lowden's River Cartwright, who collapsed at the end of season 6 and looked like he was about to die.

Season 7 should feature the team at Slough House hunting a mole inside the British government, a trope known to always add tension related to the character(s) being investigated and even within those leading the investigation. When it comes to season 8, a clash between Jackson Lamb and Diana Taverner should shake things up in a major way, continuing to make the thriller a show you never know exactly what to expect, and that is why Slow Horses delivers a masterclass in tension.

#3325. 8 Most Confusing Sci-Fi Books of All Time, Ranked

If it isn't mind-melting, it isn't sci-fi. Over the years, the science fiction genre has evolved beyond stories centered exclusively on science, often using scientific elements as a backdrop for deeply human experiences. However, sci-fi in its purest form puts science and its related fields at the forefront, exploring just how far humanity can push scientific boundaries. These ideas aren't always easy to grasp, and following the science behind it can be just as demanding as understanding the story itself.

Even the most dedicated sci-fi fans can struggle with meticulous prose, complex theories, and unconventional storytelling. Deciphering the themes is one thing, but making it through the entire book is a challenge in itself. From fragmented narratives that blur the line between reality and fiction to stories built around challenging mathematical reasoning, here are the most confusing sci-fi books of all time, ranked.

Set in the fictional American city of Bellona, Dhalgren follows a young man who arrives with no memories of himself, not even his name. Referred to as The Kid, he wanders through Bellona's streets, meets its eccentric residents, and gets involved with Lanya Colson, a woman living in a local commune. As he settles into this strange city, he begins experiencing bizarre events that blur the boundaries between time, identity, and reality.

Dhalgren's unusual literary style can take some getting used to. While Dhalgren isn't particularly difficult because of hard science or technical jargon, its fragmented, experimental prose can be confusing to follow. Readers are constantly thrown between incomplete thoughts, abstract observations, and sudden shifts in perspective. Much of the narration also follows a stream-of-consciousness style, making it hard to keep track of what's happening and differentiate between the Kid's mind and reality.

Set during the final days of World War II, Gravity's Rainbow follows American soldier Tyrone Slothrop, whose sexual encounters appear mysteriously connected to German V2 rocket strikes across London. When intelligence agencies discover this bizarre pattern, they begin monitoring him, pulling him into military conspiracies, psychological experiments, and secret Nazi research surrounding rocket technology.

Thomas Pynchon certainly doesn't skimp on characters, with the novel featuring hundreds of named individuals. Keeping track of who's who, figuring out which characters actually matter, and connecting their stories to the bigger picture can feel like homework. Still, Gravity's Rainbow has plenty of bizarre, hilarious moments to keep readers entertained, including Americans being forced to eat British candy. It's a wild ride, even when you have no idea what's going on.

Set across two different timelines, The Peripheral follows Flynne Fisher, a skilled gamer who witnesses a brutal murder while filling in for her brother on what she believes is a virtual-reality security job. Unbeknownst to her, the crime takes place in the distant future, where a London publicist named Wilf Netherton becomes entangled in a murder investigation that connects their two worlds through mysterious technological links.

If you enjoyed Netflix's Bodies, The Peripheral is an even bigger mind-bender. Besides juggling two seemingly unrelated timelines, the novel throws new characters and situations at readers without much explanation of who they are or why they matter. You're expected to figure out who's who while the plot keeps moving. William Gibson doesn't make things easier either, rarely stopping to explain what's going on.

Set on a dying Earth under a dimming red sun, The Book of the New Sun follows Severian, an apprentice torturer exiled from Nessus after showing mercy to a condemned prisoner. Armed with his executioner's sword, Terminus Est, he travels across a decaying world filled with ancient technology, strange creatures, and warring factions, slowly moving toward a destiny that could change humanity's future.

The confusing part starts with Gene Wolfe's writing style, which feels closer to 19th-century literature and is packed with obscure words that most readers won't recognize. Wolfe also describes futuristic technology using unfamiliar, old-fashioned terms. Even the appendices make it all the more confusing, presenting fictional translators' notes that claim the story was translated from a language that hasn't even come into existence yet.

Humanity's first encounter with extraterrestrial life doesn't exactly go as expected in Blindsight. Set in 2082, the novel follows five transhuman specialists sent aboard the spaceship Theseus to investigate a mysterious signal near the edge of the solar system. Their search leads them to Rorschach, a massive alien structure inhabited by creatures called Scramblers. Despite their intelligence, these beings show no signs of self-awareness, raising some pretty unsettling questions about life itself.

Peter Watts takes this strange discovery and turns it into a full-blown exploration of human consciousness. The novel gets particularly confusing when it starts challenging the very concept of consciousness, mixing complex neuroscience, evolutionary biology, and philosophical arguments into its alien encounters. The idea gets even harder to wrap your head around when the novel suggests that consciousness might actually hold humanity back.

Neal Stephenson's Anathem takes place on the planet Arbre, where scholars live in secluded monasteries called concents, dedicating their lives to science, philosophy, and mathematics. However, their untouched world is disrupted when an alien spacecraft appears in orbit. Fraa Erasmas, a young monk-in-training, joins his fellow scholars in investigating the mysterious visitors, only to discover that there's much more to their arrival than anyone expected.

The real brain workout comes from Stephenson's wild scientific ideas, which touch on consciousness, quantum physics, parallel universes, and alien civilizations. The novel also explores how mathematics might exist independently of the physical world and even shape reality. Between complicated theories, conflicting timelines, and multiple layers of existence, keeping track of what's actually happening can be a challenge.

Set in the 30th century, Diaspora imagines a future where humanity has moved far beyond its biological origins. Humans now share the world with artificial intelligences and digital minds living in simulated environments called "polises." When astronomers spot a cosmic disaster heading toward Earth, a group of physicists sets out to investigate.

It takes a serious amount of brainpower to keep up with Greg Egan's take on physics. Rather than sticking to established scientific theories, he introduces his own framework, called Kozuch Theory, to explain how particles work through some pretty unconventional ideas. The science gets increasingly difficult to wrap your head around as Egan introduces concepts that challenge everything readers know about how the universe works.

The Three-Body Problem opens during China's Cultural Revolution, when astrophysicist Ye Wenjie gets involved in a secret military project searching for extraterrestrial life. After receiving an unexpected message from an alien civilization on Trisolaris, she makes a decision that puts humanity’s future on the line. Centuries later, Earth discovers that an alien invasion is coming.

The science is already demanding enough, as Liu Cixin takes a classical physics concept and expands it into an extreme hypothesis. Imagine a planet caught between three suns, constantly shifting between extreme heat and freezing temperatures because of their unpredictable gravitational pull. The characters don't make things easier either. They're emotionally distant and often feel like vehicles for scientific discussions, with conversations that read more like lectures. Here's hoping the science and characters are easier to understand when the Netflix adaptation returns in January 2027.
