#3324. 10 Shows Like 'MobLand' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Crime dramas often attract big stars, and MobLand is no exception. The Paramount+ series stars Tom Hardy as mob fixer Harry Da Souza, with Pierce Brosnan and Paddy Considine in supporting roles and Helen Mirren having a ball as the thoroughly evil matriarch of the Harrigan crime family.

While families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family. After you've watched the recently released second season of MobLand, try one of these other shows mixing crime and family (or Family) drama.

Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. He learns that his dad was tied to various criminal enterprises, and that his scouse brother is millions of pounds in debt to a drug dealer. What else is the dapper, military-trained Duke to do but learn to navigate the violent underworld while looking cool? You won't be surprised to learn that this British crime drama comes from creator/writer/producer Guy Ritchie, who also has a hand in MobLand. Stream The Gentlemen on Netflix.

Another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's company town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the new sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated plan to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

MobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

Based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

Tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he says he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates new maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Company all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

Best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other shows on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

The great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. A more than capable crime boss in his own right, Johnson resolves to take on the Genovese crime family, eventually forming a tentative alliance with Malcolm X (Nigél Thatch and, later, Jason Alan Carvell). Johnson is the lesser evil as far as Malcolm and others are concerned, and a complicated figure as both crime lord and family man with aspirations of saving his neighborhood. The show will conclude with a two-hour finale, likely airing in 2027. Stream Godfather of Harlem on Hulu.

Adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a new adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.

#3321. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $30 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original launched all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $39.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails between $59.99 and $69.99 for a physical copy, but Nintendo is selling it for $39.99 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally launched on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $39.99 before Black Friday.

Nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

It depends! Its Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal runs from Nov. 22 through Dec. 5; the select games listed above will be on sale from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29; and digital titles will have discounts from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

Yes! The Switch 2 alone costs $499.99, so you essentially get the game for free. Mario Kart World is also one of the console's best multiplayer titles right now, so it makes sense to pick it up in this bundle.

#3314. GTA 6 Boss Gives Official Update On GTA 7

GTA 6 was such a monumentally anticipated release that everything dealing with it was under a microscope. This was the case for several other GTA games before it, once GTA 3 brought even more fame to the series. But with GTA 6, and expectations that it would be one of the biggest entertainment releases in any sector, it made sense there would be even more scrutiny.

That's ultimately part of the reason why Rockstar (under the ownership of Take-Two) decided to delay the game multiple times. Since everyone in the world would be watching when it came out, it needed a level of polish that many AAA games don't get anymore.

So imagine our surprise when GTA 7 was already mentioned, less than a week after the release of GTA 6. Speaking to Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, TBPN got an unexpected response regarding GTA 7 [via X].

Talking to Zelnick, when asked if "GTA 7 would be a live version of the entire world," Zelnick had this to say in response:

I can't help myself. We at Take-Two just went live with GTA 6 on November 19, wait let me check my watch, it's still November 19, and we're talking about GTA 7...I mean guys, really? I don't know, my father-in-law had a line whenever...he had many great business achievements...and if you ever said anything nice, he'd say those are yesterday's headlines.

“Once you get through several hundred hours of the most incredible fun you’ve ever had, ask the question again," he also noted. While it sounds rough on paper, Zelnick took the response in stride and talked about the achievements of GTA 6.

Once again, GTA 6 has entered the collective consciousness, and it's pretty much all the entertainment industry is talking about right now. There are so many moving parts in GTA 6; it's wild, especially when it comes to the Easter Eggs, secrets, and detailed recreations of South Florida's infrastructure.

Having played through the entire game, it's a true testament to how much money Rockstar is willing to throw at their game budgets. We saw this with most mainline GTA games, but Red Dead Redemption 2 also tested the limits of what AAA games could offer. With its expansive and dynamic open world, it whisked players back to a bygone era.

But with GTA 6, it's much different. The team had to recreate a modern aesthetic but also give it its own unique spin, which I think they succeeded at. After all, the world of GTA is slightly askew compared to ours, with alternate acronyms for organizations and a lot more nuances.

GTA 7 might be over a decade away at this point, but people will be talking about GTA 6 for that long, if not longer. That's definitely going to be the case whenever Rockstar gets to the next iteration of GTA Online, which is bound to happen at some point, along with the inevitable PC port.

#3313. Jon Bernthal’s 100-Minute Taylor Sheridan Thriller Is Officially Cut From Netflix

If you’ve binged Taylor Sheridan’s TV universe twice over, it’s time to check out one of his movie projects that will be leaving Netflix on December 1, making November 30 your last chance to watch. Those Who Wish Me Dead is a 2021 action thriller starring Angelina Jolie and Jon Bernthal as characters who face the worst of nature and humanity during one wild fight for survival. It features all that’s good about the Yellowstone creator’s storytelling, combined with two stars who know how to make you feel every step of their journey.

The Oscar-winning star plays Hannah Faber, a smokejumper (wildland firefighter) in the Montana wilderness who is haunted by a past failure that cost lives. Now living in isolation, her simple routine is shattered when she encounters Connor (Finn Little), a young man who witnesses a murder and now has the killers on his tail. Hannah must use all of her experience to navigate a forest which is being ravaged by a wildfire, in order to evade capture and confront the demons of her past.

It is the third film to be directed by Sheridan, who also co-wrote the script, and has been compared to cult ‘90s survival thrillers like Cliffhanger and The River Wild, where nature becomes as foreboding as the villains. Hannah and Connor’s every turn is blocked by a new life-or-death challenge, with the emotional stakes being raised constantly. It’s an entertaining story of redemption, elevated by the traits that made Sheridan a TV mogul.

Sheridan has shown strength as a director of mid-budget dramas and thrillers intended for adult audiences.

Taylor Sheridan had already scored big with Yellowstone at the time of the film’s release, starting down a path that would see him become synonymous with big stars, big ranches, and even bigger plot twists. Those Who Wish Me Dead has a different setting, but there’s so much in the story that is typical of what Sheridan does best. His signature themes of blue-collar heroics, the burden of responsibility, and frontier morality are all present, as are low-key protagonists who are reluctantly drawn back into a world that forces them to deal with the past.

He delivers action free of the fantasy trappings of genre cinema. You won’t find any special powers or enchanted weapons here, just the will to survive and the force of ordinary people pushed to the limit. Sheridan would write more celebrated movies, such as the crime thriller Hell or High Water and the Sicario films, but if you’re a completist of his work, then this is a cinematic adventure his fans won’t regret seeking out.

Since his breakthrough on the TV show The Walking Dead, Bernthal has specialized in gritty, working-class characters who have more depth than their gruff exteriors suggest. Whether it’s the vigilante fury of The Punisher, the calculating criminality of his role in Baby Driver, or his striking appearance in The Odyssey, he is someone who can bring a lot of impact no matter how high he is on the call sheet.

Those Who Wish Me Dead is no exception, as he holds his own with one of Hollywood’s biggest stars. He plays Ethan Sawyer, a sheriff’s deputy who becomes part of the chase and an ally to Hannah. In many ways, he is a classic Taylor Sheridan hero – a quiet man who does the right thing and gets the job done in order to save innocent lives. He is a direct counterpoint to the villains, in that he is a thoroughly decent man who puts himself in danger to do the right thing. It’s not a huge role in the movie, but it gives an extra human element to a set-piece-heavy movie.

Those Who Wish Me Dead didn’t find the audience it deserved upon release, arriving as the world was still recovering from the 2020 pandemic and people were still reluctant to return to theaters. However, given Sheridan’s status only seems to go from strength to strength, people who want to see even more from him will find everything they love about his TV work in 100 action-packed minutes.

#3311. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In all the years you've been online, you've likely created more accounts than you can remember, whether to shop on a website you made one purchase from, sign up for a newsletter you've since stopped reading, or download apps for school or work that you no longer need.

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

The next place to look is in your email: Search for account confirmation and verification emails as well as password resets using keywords like "verify your email," "free trial," "welcome," "confirm your account," or "sign up." Add a date filter to narrow down older accounts. Do this across all of your email addresses.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

#3309. Report: Apple job listings detail plans for autonomous AI agents

Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the company’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted new job listings that offer a closer look at its plans to develop autonomous AI agents:

In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the company could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how quickly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally launched its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

#3308. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

#3306. The Best Tech Deals From the Sam's Club Early Black Friday Sale

Retailers are churning out early Black Friday deals already, including the likes of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and others. If you're waiting around for Friday, Nov. 27 to do all of your shopping, you might miss out on some deals and unnecessarily make the day more stressful than it needs to be. If you're a Sam's Club member, you have access to many early Black Friday deals worth checking out. I spent some time combing through their website and rounded up my favorite tech deals below.

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

Gaming monitors can get expensive quickly, but you can get decent options on a budget. A great example is the 31.5-inch MSi gaming monitor selling for $129 (originally $179). It has a 250Hz refresh rate and a 1ms response time to make gaming smoother. There's also AMD FreeSync Premium to get rid of tearing and stuttering.

These kinds of sales are always a good time to upgrade laptops. If you're looking for a powerful computer that is well-rounded, consider the 16-inch HP OmniBook 7 Flip going for $699 (originally $899). This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

If you need a bigger screen, the 17.3-inch HP OmniBook 3 is a good choice for a bit less money. It comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 12GB of RAM. Part of the bigger screen means a bigger keyboard, so if you deal with numbers a lot, you'd likely appreciate the numeric pad.

If you want your laptop strictly for gaming, the ASUS TUF F16 Gaming laptop is $1,149 (originally $1,399). With an Intel Core 7 processor and the RTX 5060 graphics card, you'll be well set up to tackle heavy games. It comes with a 165Hz refresh rate, Advanced Arc Flow fans and vents to keep your machine cool, and 16GB DDR5 RAM to keep your loads short.

Budget TVs get big discounts during Black Friday, and the 58-inch Vizio QLED TV is one of them. You can get one for $178 (originally $298), and it supports Dolby Vision HDR for better color and contrast. The operating system is the Vizio OS, but of course, you can always change it with a TV dongle if you prefer a different one.

If you prefer to splurge for a better QLED but still get a good deal, the 65-inch Samsung QN90H QLED TV at $1,197.99 (originally $1,497.99) is a great option. It upscales lower-resolution pictures to 4K with AI. It works for gaming with its 144Hz refresh rate, and because the operating system is Tizen OS, it comes with Samsung TV Plus, which brings over 2,700 free channels. The TV also comes with Dolby Atmos, so you can hear audio with a 3D effect as the audio follows objects around the display.

A 100-inch TV makes a statement: You take your entertainment system seriously. The 100-inch Vizio QLED TV is a budget-friendly option with a $300 discount, currently going for $1,198 (originally $1,498). This TV supports Dolby Vision HDR for more vivid images and has hundreds of free channels with the Vizio OS.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3304. 62-Episode Prime Video Sci-Fi Series Only Gets Better With Age

Time is as cruel to sci-fi television as it is to humans. As more time goes by, it becomes hard not to notice how sci-fi shows that were once considered masterpieces are slowly decaying into tomorrow's relics. Good sci-fi storytelling alone remains timeless. However, from a visual and legacy standpoint, many TV shows of our time struggle to sustain what they started.

Fortunately, Prime Video's The Expanse is a rare exception.

Perhaps in a decade, even the visuals from The Expanse will start feeling dated. The CGI from earlier seasons already seems a little rough around the edges. Yet, overall, The Expanse can still stand well against some of the biggest big-screen productions. The reason being that its visual language emphasized grounded physics and industrial grit instead of extreme photorealism.

When it comes to The Expanse's themes, it feels more relevant than ever. Its portrayal of manufactured class divides, information war, and humanity's unchecked ambition reflects real concerns surrounding today's world. Beyond its themes and visuals, however, there is another aspect that ensures the Prime Video sci-fi show ages like George Clooney.

Way too many sci-fi shows have landed in the ever-growing graveyard of the streaming era's cancelations. This has happened to a point where many viewers have even given up on getting too invested in shows. After all, one can never know when the proverbial plug will be pulled.

The Expanse, too, almost became a victim of the same trend. Despite earning immense acclaim after landing on Syfy, it was canceled after just three seasons. History could have repeated itself. The Expanse could have become another forgotten sci-fi series that fell short of reaching its full potential.

However, this is when fan-campaigning and Amazon eventually saved the day.

More often than not, fan campaigns go unnoticed. When the economics stop making sense, streaming services and networks care little about fan campaigns from cult audiences. In The Expanse's case, though, fans did everything from flying a place over Amazon Studios to launching a miniature Rocinante into near-space.

As a result, The Expanse was saved by Amazon, and Jeff Bezos himself announced its return. He said (via Forbes),

"I just got word that The Expanse is saved. The show is extraordinary, and these guys are unbelievably talented.”

While Prime Video, too, could not eventually sustain the show's run beyond season 6, it is hard not to be grateful that The Expanse got to last so long. Some of the best aspects of the series emerge after season 3, which shows how it would not have been half as good if Prime Video had not given it a second chance.

Unlike many canceled sci-fi shows, The Expanse has a reliable 6-season arc with a solid legacy. It continues to age so well because it got the opportunity to reach its full potential.

Lined up with the same team as The Expanse, Prime Video is adapting Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck's The Captive's War book series. Naren Shankar of The Expanse fame is returning as the showrunner, while director Breck Eisner is also set to helm the series. Reports suggest that even Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck​​​​ are actively involved in the series' writers' room.

With so much going in The Captive's War's favor, it is hard not to hope that it will get the same treatment as The Expanse. Unlike The Expanse, The Captive's War only consists of a trilogy of books. Owing to this, if its creators adapt only one book per season, the show could wrap its run in just three seasons.

However, given how unpredictable streaming cancellations have become, one can only pray that it will last long enough to cover its entire source material. Given the strength of its production team and source material, though, The Captive's War could have a strong three-to-four season run before concluding its story.

#3303. 'SilverFin's Full-Cast Audiobook Is an Immersive Look at the Boy Who Would Be Bond | Review

There’s officially a new James Bond on the big screen in the shape of Robert Pattinson, which means there’s a whole new 007 to spend the next few years speculating about. There’s also a new Bond to listen to right now, and he’s still a schoolboy. The fun of Big Finish’s SilverFin is hearing how much of the iconic spy is already there at thirteen, although it's fair to say the production is in absolutely no rush to introduce us to him.

In fact, it spends nearly ten minutes with two children, Alfie and Jeannie, on a fishing trip that will initially have you thinking, "where's the Bond boy?" However, Joe Kraemer’s score and Benji Clifford’s sound design are so striking that they give the loch just enough time to go from peaceful to ominous. Then there's an attack, and then something attacks, the new theme kicks in, and suddenly it sounds like Bond.

Isaac Rouse (The Crown) plays James in the full-cast audio adaptation of SilverFin, the first novel in Charlie Higson’s Young Bond series, produced by Big Finish and Ian Fleming Publications. Higson takes Bond back to the 1930s, when he’s a new boy at Eton. Instead of global annihilation, his biggest problem here is a bully with a rich father. Imagine. Then James goes to Scotland for the holidays, the children’s disappearance becomes his first real mystery, and it's not the bully that's the big problem; it's the rich daddy.

The remainder of the cast includes Charlotte McBurney as Wilder Lawless, Charlie Higson as Michael Merriot, Tim McInnerny as Max Bond, Miranda Raison as Charmian Bond, Miriam Margolyes as Cleek MacSawney, William Hope as Lord Randolph Hellebore, Christopher Nathan as George Hellebore, Paterson Joseph as Dr. Perseus Friend, Harry Marcus as Red Kelly, Lucy Fleming as Madame Ouspenskaya, Timothy Bentinck as Sergeant White, and Penelope Rawlins as Alfie Kelly.

Spanning 8 hours across 16 episodes, the adaptation has been helmed by writer and director Barnaby Edwards, and he wisely makes the decision to give James time to settle into both worlds. After all, there's an entire school sporting competition to get through, and at one point Uncle Max explains how a Rolls-Royce engine works in frankly ridiculous detail. The scene has every right to be boring, and yet, it’s fascinating, partly because Max takes such pleasure in explaining it and partly because James perks up once he realizes how many little explosions it takes to make a car go. That’s SilverFin at its best. It gives its characters time to enjoy one another’s company, which makes it hurt all the more when things go horribly wrong.

Now, Rouse is a hard sell as a 13-year-old boy, and even more so when the story flashes back to an even younger James. Yet, by the end of the Hellebore Cup, you cannot imagine anyone else doing the role. The things that pop out instantly are the charm, that basically obnoxious and undeserved confidence he has at that age, and the way he's still figuring out how far a witty line can get him.

Rishi Manuel’s Pritpal Nandra gives the Eton episodes their warmth. He explains the school to James and the listener in one go, in a moment that actually feels very "Basil Exposition," if you want to feel extra Bond-meta. Their teasing feels like two boys actually becoming friends, and there’s room for another episode of that before the Hellebore Cup takes over. After two episodes of George Hellebore being an absolute Malfoy of a boy, hearing James overtake him is wildly satisfying. Then George has to face his father, and suddenly third place feels like the worst thing that could have happened to him.

Perhaps the heart of the Scottish scenes is when James and his Uncle Max go fishing, something you wouldn't think could be that compelling in an audio drama — yet, it is. McInnerny is just great here, and he brings that same easy charm and warmth to the scene where Max tells James about working as a spy during the war, as well as how he got the limp he came home with. Miranda Raison’s Aunt Charmian makes it easy to see why coming back to this family matters to James, especially after the surprisingly affecting flashbacks to his parents.

Red Kelly’s return is a delight, and Wilder Lawless makes such an immediate impression that it’s a shame she takes more than three hours to turn up. And then there’s Meatpacker Moran, a name that deserves to go down in history, whom Stuart Milligan makes unexpectedly good company. The first half’s finale spends most of its time following him, James, and Red around the outside of Castle Hellebore. Clifford’s sound design makes the grounds easy to picture, so there’s time to appreciate the sheer scale of the place and how much trouble the boys will be in once they go inside.

William Hope makes Lord Randolph Hellebore vile from the moment he opens his mouth, and Miriam Margolyes makes his gamekeeper frightening enough to carry a scene on her own. Even in that company, Paterson Joseph is something else as Doctor Perseus Friend. He talks to George about eugenics and mass death like they've just caught up for coffee in Cafe Nervosa in Seattle. Later, he manages to make the simple prospect of watching someone eat sound deeply sinister. A plan to create super-soldiers using eels sounds gloriously daft on paper, but Joseph makes it disturbing by playing Friend as a man who’s found an excuse to do exactly what he wants to do.

The laboratory episodes spend a long time explaining what Hellebore is doing, and by the later chapters a few of Kraemer’s cues have become a little too familiar. “The Future of Warfare” still lands hard enough to make a break between episodes feel welcome. Edwards gives away very little about what happened to Alfie and Jeannie. Those first ten minutes on the loch do a lot of the work. By the time James and George start smashing up the laboratory in “Hellfire,” it’s a punch-the-air moment. George’s change of heart happens quickly, but Christopher Nathan has been letting the fear slip through his arrogance since Eton.

And then there’s Uncle Max. The series gives plenty of reason to suspect he’ll die, and his letter is still an absolute gut punch. He’s reminding James how to start the car one moment and telling him how much those last few days together meant to him the next. Then Charmian says, “How lucky we are,” even as she’s grieving him. It’s a lovely way to end their time in Scotland.

SilverFin is an enjoyable, impressively atmospheric start for Big Finish’s Young Bond, but its eight-hour runtime gives the uneven pacing plenty of room to show. The school adventures and quieter family scenes build an appealing world around James, but lengthy laboratory explanations slow the story just when it should be gathering momentum. The irony is that, in reviewing this audio adaptation, the strongest praise goes to the performances, direction, and sound design, while the biggest frustrations lie with a story that’s been around for two decades and is showing its creaks. However, Isaac Rouse’s charm, a strong supporting cast, and Benji Clifford’s vivid soundscape do a lot of the heavy lifting, while the emotional finale delivers a proper gut punch, rounding off a promising debut for Big Finish.

Superb performances and atmospheric audio production make SilverFin an engaging Young Bond debut, though the decades-old story shows its weaknesses through uneven pacing and lengthy exposition.

#3302. Ex-NFL Star Shawne Merriman's Company Asks Judge to Uphold Removing Him From Leadership Positions

Shawne Merriman's own company wants him ousted ... and its leadership has gone to a federal judge to get it done ASAP.

A.R.I. Agent and the company Lights Out -- Merriman's combat sports company -- claim that Merriman defaulted on millions of dollars worth of loans ... and the companies say A.R.I. was then contractually allowed to take over the company and oust Merriman from all leadership positions.

They also claim that Merriman misled A.R.I. to obtain the loan ... claiming he did not tell them some assets were already being used as collateral against other loans -- and they alleged he misrepresented which companies owned what intellectual property.

Basically, A.R.I. says Merriman had two different companies with basically the same name ... one of which held the intellectual property they wanted to acquire.

On top of all that, A.R.I. claims Merriman never disclosed the wrongful death lawsuit he was facing ... which the company claims would have affected his ability to secure a loan.

A.R.I. isn't asking the judge to rule on the entire lawsuit ... the company just wants the judge to uphold their legal claim to Lights Out and to clear up the intellectual property confusion.

As we reported ... Merriman and three others have been ordered to pay $4 million in connection with the 2017 death of Kimberly Fattorini.

Remember ... Fattorini was found dead with alcohol, cocaine and GHB found in her system. She allegedly texted a friend that she believed Merriman put GHB in her drink. Merriman has always denied all wrongdoing.

We've reached out to Merriman about A.R.I.'s filing ... so far, no word back.

#3299. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

#3297. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. #3293. 5 Classic Books Better Than 'Moby-Dick'

At any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention. He’ll never turn down a campus novel with a literary bent, nor will he hesitate to add yet another mystery to his Leaning Tower of Pisa-inspired to-be-read pile — which is built upon the bedrocks of too many short story collections, how-are-these-real true crime books, and classics waiting to be cracked open again. Topics that have him ripping through pages the fastest include closed-circle murders, unhappy professors, life-questioning philosophical deep dives, so long as they feature sharp sentences, a dark sense of humor, and at least a little malice.

He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.

It's hard to describe Moby-Dick. On the surface, it's a simple story of revenge, about a ship captain hunting the whale that took his leg. But the novel comes in waves. There are chapters about whale anatomy and the whaling industry. There's an entire chapter devoted to the color white. These chapters, at times, drown the whole whale hunting business until it once again bobs its head above it all. Yet all that diving and resurfacing is what made Moby Dick such uncharted territory. Herman Melville hooks you with the promise of adventure, but it's the examination of obsession, of fate, and of man's relationship with nature that continues reeling you in. It's an attempt to understand and to make sense of the world, and it reads part adventure, part encyclopedia, part philosophical argument. And somehow it all works.

That's what the greatest novels manage to do. They use a simple story — about a man, about a family, about one small part of the world — as the basis to explore so much more. They make us care about people we might otherwise despise, or they find tragedy in the ridiculous. They don't need to be so obviously about absolutely everything as Melville was. Some manage an extraordinary amount with very little. Some sprawl across generations, taking us so far from where we began that it's difficult to believe we're still reading the same book. So, sure, Moby-Dick deserves its place among the greatest novels ever written. But it's hardly the only one to make an improbable story into something extraordinary; and a few have managed to do it even better.

Don Quixote has become something of a punch line. A sort of shorthand for anyone undertaking an obviously outlandish pursuit. It’s about an aging man who reads one too many stories about knights. He decides he ought to become one himself and heads off to fight giants that turn out to be windmills. It's all a little ridiculous. But while Miguel de Cervantes' deluded knight is farcical, he has a way of exposing some truths. Yes, he's hopelessly out of touch with reality; but, he still believes in honor and justice, and takes it upon himself to defend anyone who needs protection.

Then there's Sancho Panza. A grand promise of an island to govern sends him trotting alongside Don Quixote. We're to think he's the sensible one despite that. After all, he knows that windmills aren't giants. Yet he follows Don Quixote from one absurd adventure to the next. He argues with him, sure, but he also loves to indulge Don Quixote. He even has the tendency to get caught up in all the nonsense goings-on himself. As the whole thing unfolds, it becomes harder and harder to pinpoint who the actual fool is. Because it's the people who humiliate Don Quixote that have a much uglier view of the world, and we're not talking about his tendency to see castles where everyone sees inns. Like Melville's Ahab, he's a man possessed by an idea, unwilling to accept anything that contradicts it. But where Ahab's obsession leaves death and destruction in its wake, Don Quixote's produces something altogether more complicated.

Rodion Raskolnikov has a theory: the usual rules of morality don't apply to certain men. They're just a bit too special. Napoleon didn't get where he did by worrying about all the people who died along the way. And Raskolnikov, a penniless former student living in St. Petersburg, decides he might belong to that exclusive club. So he decides to test his little theory and murders an elderly pawnbroker, reasoning that her money could be put to better use. Then he murders her sister, too.

But the murders take up little of Crime and Punishment. The real story is about Raskolnikov trying to get on with his life afterward. He's feverish and he's paranoid. He's insufferable to the few people who still give a damn about him. He panics after perfectly innocent conversations. Every encounter with Porfiry Petrovich, the magistrate investigating the murders, is fraught with tension; not only the pitter and the patter between the two, but internally as he contemplates whether he's about to be arrested or merely imagining things. Raskolnikov, like Melville's Ahab, has convinced himself he's somehow above the rest of humanity. But unlike Ahab's obsession dragging an entire ship toward disaster, it's Raskolnikov dragging himself, and only himself, into demise.

Middlemarch sounds like a hard sell. Nearly 800 pages about the goings-on in a provincial English town. People marry the wrong people. They borrow money. They gossip, and they meddle in one another's affairs. There's not exactly a whale to chase. But there is Dorothea Brooke, who's desperate to do something with her life. She convinces herself she can help Edward Casaubon, an older scholar, produce some great intellectual work. And so she marries him. There's just one little issue to contend with: Casaubon isn't nearly as brilliant as she imagines.

What makes Middlemarch engrossing is how decisions tend to become someone else's problem. A marriage made with the best intentions turns miserable. A few unpaid bills threaten to derail a promising career. And a bit of gossip, passed from one drawing room to another, can do more damage than anyone intended. Nobody is entirely innocent in all this, though few are outright villains. Even the most infuriating characters have their reasons for behaving as they do, and we get to see how they came by them. George Eliot gives us an entire town of people pursuing their own ideas of happiness, often at the expense of someone else's. Melville sends Ahab halfway around the world to examine the forces that govern human lives; Eliot hardly needs to leave the confines of a small English town.

Britain makes more detective television than any country has any business making, and somehow almost all of it is good. Here is the one you belong in, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You want the tea, the gossip and the vicar behaving oddly. Midsomer is a county where the scenery is beautiful, the fete is on Saturday and the murder rate is roughly that of a small war, and absolutely nobody involved thinks this is strange.

You feel other people's grief as if it were handed to you personally. Broadchurch is less a whodunnit than a study of what a small town does to itself when it finds out that the answer was always going to be somebody everybody already knew.

You go through things rather than around them. John Luther is the best detective in London and a liability to everybody who works with him, and the show is completely honest that those two facts are the same fact.

You say the thing and you do not dress it up. Vera Stanhope turns up in a hat and a mac, is rude to almost everybody, and is the only person in the room prepared to ask the question that the family has been waiting years for somebody to ask.

Germinal takes us underground. Deep underground, into the coal mines of northern France. Émile Zola introduces us to Étienne Lantier, who finds work at Le Voreux, a mine that's been swallowing generations of workers. Take the Maheu family. Nearly everyone works in the mines, yet there's hardly enough money to put food on the table. They spend their days risking their lives. They come home exhausted, get up the next day to dig. Rinse, repeat. All the while, the mine owners live a comfortable existence. So when the company makes an already miserable existence even harder, Étienne helps organize a strike.

But refusing to work means no food. As the strike drags on, the cupboards empty. Families who barely had enough to begin with now have nothing. Solidarity amongst the miners fractures. Some want to hold out. Others are desperate to get back to work. People who've spent their lives working alongside one another are turning against each other. There's anger and there’s violence. That's what makes Germinal so devastating. Zola gives us an entire community whose lives are dictated by the work that's slowly killing them. Like Melville, he's interested in man's struggle against forces much bigger than himself. But while Ahab drags his crew halfway around the world to confront the source of his misery, Zola's miners have to descend into theirs every morning.

Good luck keeping track of the Buendía family in One Hundred Years of Solitude. The foliage that the various José Arcadios and Aurelianos alone occupy on the family tree is astounding. And that's before getting into all the strange things happening around them. An outbreak of insomnia leaves people forgetting the names of everyday objects, so they start sticking labels on everything. A young woman floats off to heaven while folding bedsheets. The dead occasionally stop by for a visit. And nobody seems particularly bothered by any of it. In Gabriel García Márquez's world, the impossible is just another part of everyday life.

But the names aren't the only things that keep repeating. Over seven generations, the Buendías fall into the same traps as their parents and grandparents. They pursue doomed romances and they nurse old grudges. They throw themselves into grand ambitions that inevitably come to very little. And their hometown of Macondo experiences its own troubles. There are civil wars. There are political upheavals. There's the arrival of a foreign banana company. When striking workers are massacred, the authorities insist it never happened. And before long, almost everyone seems to believe them. Where Melville uses the pursuit of a single whale to examine mankind's place in the world, García Márquez gives us a century of births, deaths, wars, and family squabbles to explore how history gets repeated, distorted, and sometimes forgotten altogether.
